h: In the name of purification: the marginalised are being pushed off the voter rolls
dek: Writing in Al Jazeera, sociologist Tanweer Fazal argues that the SIR has become an exercise not in cleaning up the voter list but in creating two tiers of citizenship.
body: Sociology professor Tanweer Fazal begins on the streets of Delhi, where thousands of people came out over the weekend against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and faced a heavy police crackdown and mass detentions. In his view, one number lies at the root of this anger: during the Special Intensive Revision, or SIR, more than 13 crore (130 million) names were removed from the voter rolls.

The author accepts that revising the rolls is nothing unusual in itself. New voters are added, and the names of people who have died or moved elsewhere are removed. But he says this revision is unprecedented in its scale, its arbitrary process and the exclusion it has caused. The Commission and the ruling party call it shuddhi, or purification, and to the author that word is itself worrying in a society divided by caste.

His main argument is that the process is designed not to include as many people as possible but to exclude as many as possible. At first Aadhaar was left out of the list of valid documents. Then demands for educational certificates, land papers and family trees put the burden of proof on poor voters. In Bengal, of the nearly 90 lakh (9 million) names removed, 27 lakh (2.7 million) fell into a category called "logical discrepancy", decided by an AI-based system that matches names against old lists. Women who changed their name or address after marriage are the easiest to catch in it.

According to the author, the burden was not shared equally. In Bengal, about 65 percent of those removed under this category were reported to be Muslim, while there are only 19 tribunals for more than 38 lakh (3.8 million) appeals. He cites figures from Hyderabad and Delhi-NCR that point the same way. Using Bihar as an example, he says that in 2020 the gap between the two alliances was very slim, but after 68 lakh (6.8 million) names were removed, the BJP alliance's lead in 2025 rose to nearly nine points.

Finally, the author places the SIR in a chain that includes Assam's NRC, the 2019 Citizenship Amendment Act and the new high-level committee on demographic change. His conclusion is that it is one of several tools through which some groups are first made suspect, then voiceless, and finally pushed to the margins of citizenship.
nazar: The Jantar Mantar protest is often presented as a demand for one officer's resignation. This article reminds us that the real question is about the crores of people whose names were quietly struck off, especially Muslims, migrant workers and women, who have the fewest papers. Many of the article's figures come from different analyses and need independent checking, but the question of who bore the burden cannot be put off.
The vote is the poorest person's only equality. If even that is made conditional on papers, the structure of democracy stays standing while it is hollowed out from within.
sawal: Who will speak for the person whose name was struck off?
ref: SIR
Special Intensive Revision: the Election Commission's fresh check of the voter rolls. The last intensive revision was held in 2003-04.
Logical discrepancy
A category in Bengal's SIR under which a name was questioned if the details of the name or family relations did not match the old list.

h: The fight for democracy is in the hands of the cockroaches
dek: In Jacobin, journalist Prajwal Bhat argues that the Cockroach Janata Party movement, which began as a joke, has become the most serious challenge to the Modi government, and that the government's own crackdown proves it.
body: Writing in Jacobin, New York-based journalist Prajwal Bhat says the Cockroach Janata Party was born from an online joke after Chief Justice Surya Kant called unemployed young people cockroaches. That same joke is now the most serious challenge facing Narendra Modi's government. On 10 October Delhi was turned into a fortress: more than twenty thousand police and paramilitary personnel, the internet shut down in central Delhi, and thousands detained, including CJP leaders and opposition MPs.

At the heart of the article is the Special Intensive Revision, or SIR, of the voter rolls. According to the author, it turned the whole process upside down: earlier, officials went from house to house to verify voters, but now voters must prove their own eligibility with documents. Critics say about 13 crore (130 million) names have been left out of the draft rolls. In West Bengal, nearly 90 lakh (9 million) names were cut before the April election, 34 percent of them Muslim, while Muslims make up 27 percent of the population. Of about 25 lakh (2.5 million) appeals, fewer than 3 percent have been decided, and in nearly 90 percent of those the names were restored.

Bhat also points to how the Election Commission is set up. A law passed in December 2023 increased the government's say in choosing commissioners and gave them legal immunity, and Gyanesh Kumar is the first Chief Election Commissioner appointed under it. He cites an Indian Express report that the other two commissioners recorded at least fourteen objections and were sidelined.

The author does not see this anger as only about elections. In 2025, more than 1.2 crore (12 million) people applied for 8,868 railway jobs, and a growth rate of 7.7 percent cannot hide unemployment, costly fuel and inequality. Organisers like AISA president Neha Bora have turned this restlessness into a question of accountability.

Finally, Bhat recalls that the same thing happened with the movements against the citizenship law and the farm laws: smears, force and arrests under anti-terror laws. The arrest of Sourav Das and Ashutosh Ranka while they held the national flag weakens the government's own propaganda about foreign agents. In his view, the government's response itself shows how seriously it takes this challenge.
nazar: This article rests more on figures than on slogans, and that is where its strength lies. When names are restored in ninety percent of the decided appeals in Bengal, the question arises: on what basis are the remaining lakhs of people, who have not even been heard, kept off the list?

Bhat's sharpest point is that the movement cannot be seen apart from unemployment and exam scams. When a generation that has already lost out on jobs now seems to be losing its vote too, taking to the streets is only natural.
sawal: If you have to prove your own eligibility, are you an equal citizen?
ref: Special Intensive Revision (SIR)
A nationwide check of voter rolls begun in June 2025. Voters must fill in a form and submit papers to show their link to the 2002-04 rolls.
Chief Election Commissioner law (2023)
A law that removed the Chief Justice from the panel that picks commissioners, giving the government more weight, and also gave commissioners immunity from legal action.

h: Why is crushing protest the only agenda?
dek: An editorial in Siasat, the Hyderabad Urdu daily, asks what a government that uses police force to suppress every protest against Gyanesh Kumar is really afraid of.
body: Siasat's editorial points straight at the central government, and especially the Home Ministry. In its view, the government seems to have only one priority right now: to silence every voice raised against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, whether in Delhi or in any BJP-ruled state.

The paper lists how Delhi was turned into a police camp as soon as a protest at Jantar Mantar was announced. There was heavy deployment and a show of force at other places in the city too. At one place, a petition by local traders was used to try to stop a sit-in, and an attempt to protest at India Gate was also foiled. The editorial reminds readers that the Constitution gives the right to peaceful protest and to dissent within the law, yet the government shows no tolerance at all for it.

The young members of the Cockroach Janata Party who waved the national flag and raised slogans at Jantar Mantar were arrested and sent to jail. When the party announced a Tiranga March (national flag march) for 16 October, restrictions were placed on that too. According to the editorial, the Delhi High Court expressed displeasure at these restrictions, refused to stop the march and asked the government to explain its reasons.

The editorial argues that the charges of election irregularities against Gyanesh Kumar cannot be taken lightly. Citing a media report, it says that even his fellow election commissioners have voiced their unhappiness. The paper claims that more than 13 crore (130 million) voters across the country have lost their right to vote, lakhs more fear their names will be cut, and many people shown as dead on paper are coming before the media alive. In its view, this is a mockery of democracy and a conspiracy to hollow it out.

Finally, the editorial says the government fears that if the protests grow stronger, its foundations could shake, and the methods by which, as the paper alleges, it won power could be exposed. Voices demanding democratic rights will keep rising, and attempts to crush them will fail.
nazar: This voice from the Urdu press matters because it sees the protest not as one party's affair but as a question of citizens' rights. The examples from different places form a single picture: refuse permission, take away the space, and do not back down even after a rebuke from the court.

The figure of 13 crore is the paper's own claim and needs independent checking. But if living people really are being declared dead, it is the Election Commission that must answer, not the young people on the street.
sawal: When a government fears protest this much, what is it really afraid of?
ref: Tiranga March (16 October)
The Cockroach Janata Party's call for a peaceful march in Delhi carrying the national flag. Police placed restrictions on it, and the High Court asked the government to respond.

h: Modi's real trouble lies in the streets far from the protests
dek: In Scroll, Supriya Sharma argues that the protests against the Election Commission have exposed a wider discontent, full of rising prices, joblessness and fatigue, that wants change even without an alternative in sight.
body: Scroll's Supriya Sharma went far from the protest sites, to the lanes, shops and dhabas (roadside eateries) of Delhi and Uttar Pradesh, and came back with one argument: the Modi government's bigger challenge is not the protests against the Election Commission but the broad discontent these protests have brought to the surface. The most common complaint is rising prices, and many people want change even without a clear alternative, though the general election is still about two and a half years away.

A jeweller in Karol Bagh, whose shop stayed empty because of the restrictions on 10 October, calls it a nuisance but sympathises with the protesters. Despite voting in Delhi all his life, he received an SIR notice. He feels something is wrong with the voting system. That night 45 metro stations, including Kashmere Gate, were locked, and people eating there say onions cost 80 rupees and sugar has gone from 50 to 70.

A cloth trader recalls that in 2014 the BJP used to raise the issue of petrol at 65 rupees; now it is over a hundred, and cooking gas has gone from 400 to 1,000 rupees. A labourer from Jamui in Bihar says farmers sell wheat at 20 rupees a kilo and buy it back at 32. His companions call the BJP's win in Bihar vote theft, which is their own allegation.

Two young Dalits from Uttar Pradesh believe that if elections were held with ballot papers, the BJP would be wiped out, but they also say free rations have drawn some Dalits towards the BJP. Meanwhile, a jeweller who supports the BJP asks who the opposition's common leader is. The writer herself notes that BJP supporters are counting on a divided opposition.

The article also records anger over the cost of medical treatment and inequality in education. Over the past decade, more than 90 thousand government schools have closed under a merger policy. An elderly Jat woman does not know what the protests are about, yet she is with them, because, she says, food has gone out of reach.
nazar: This article reminds us that the anger at Jantar Mantar is not alone. When a shopkeeper stands with the protesters despite his own losses, the government's argument that the movement only causes trouble for ordinary people grows weak.
But the article's limits are clear too: these are voices from the streets, not a survey. There is discontent but no alternative, and that is the biggest test for the opposition.
sawal: How far can discontent go without an alternative?
ref: School mergers
A policy of merging government schools with low enrolment into nearby schools. Critics say it puts schools further away for poor children.

h: Who gained and who lost on the street
dek: In ETV Bharat, Sachin Sharma assesses that in the Delhi protests the government gave the Cockroach Janata Party no room this time, Neha Bora shone the most, the Congress got headlines, but the real test will be the 2027 elections.
body: The writer tallies who gained and who lost from the movement against Gyanesh Kumar that has been on Delhi's streets since 10 October. His first conclusion is that the government came fully prepared this time to box in the Cockroach Janata Party, which had already forced Dharmendra Pradhan to resign through the NEET paper leak protests in July. It was refused permission at Jantar Mantar. Abhijeet Dipke, Sourav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were picked up as soon as they got off their flights, and when the condition of a peace bond was broken, Sourav and Ashutosh were sent to Tihar for five days.

According to the article, the police this time avoided open lathi (baton) charges and pellets, and put women officers in front. With the party's leaders absent from the field, media attention turned to AISA president Neha Bora, who kept up flash protests in Connaught Place and the Parliament area from 10 to 13 October. Seeing her closeness to Rahul and Priyanka Gandhi, the writer also speculates that she may follow a path like Kanhaiya Kumar's.

On 12 October the Congress marched towards the Supreme Court with several thousand people. The writer says that because of about a dozen errors in its petition, it was not listed at first; after corrections, the court issued notice. He alleges that the Home Ministry went easy on the Congress, while Cockroach Janata Party members were not even allowed to gather in one place.

The opposition's big leaders, Rahul Gandhi, Akhilesh Yadav, Tejashwi Yadav, Mamata Banerjee, Arvind Kejriwal, Sanjay Raut and Pinarayi Vijayan, were detained and quickly released, so that no one got a martyrdom story. Meanwhile, in the festive season, traders in central Delhi longed for customers, and the government removed Jantar Mantar from the list of protest sites and suggested Ramlila Maidan, Burari and the CBD Ground in Shahdara instead. These are far from Parliament and cost thousands to lakhs of rupees a day to rent.

The writer's final test is electoral. In the recent by-elections, the BJP-NDA won four of six seats, and the BJP took 38 of 44 seats in the Gandhinagar Municipal Corporation. In his view, the elections in five states in February-March 2027 will show how seriously voters take the opposition's arguments.
nazar: This article is not a slogan for the movement but a cool reckoning, and that is its value. It shows that the government learned from its July mistake: fewer batons, more detentions, catch the leaders and let them go, and take away the protest site itself.

But measuring the movement's success only by by-election and municipal seats is an incomplete yardstick. The question is about the voter rolls and the credibility of the Election Commission, and if that itself is in doubt, election results are not the answer to the question but part of it.
sawal: When the Commission itself is in question, how can its elections be the test of the movement?
ref: Peace bond
A bond signed before a magistrate promising to keep the peace for a set period. Breaking the condition can lead to detention.

h: The cockroach generation and the myth of the largest democracy
dek: In Daily Sabah, Shahmir Ghiasuddin Khan argues that it is the government's job, not the citizen's, to provide proof for every decision to remove a name from the voter list, and that batons do not change people's minds.
body: Shahmir Ghiasuddin Khan, a news editor who writes on geopolitics for the Turkish paper Daily Sabah, opens his piece on India's movement with a simple question: how can a democracy in which crores of people cannot vote represent its citizens? Thousands of young people linked to the Cockroach Janata Party are demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, and the government is responding with mass detentions and heavy security.

Citing Indian media reports, the writer says that more than 13 crore (130 million) names were removed in the revision that began last year. The Commission points to dead, relocated and missing voters and denies any political motive. According to Khan, no solid evidence has been offered for these purges. His central argument is that the burden of proving that each removal was clear, fair and open to checking lies with the authorities, not with the citizen who has to fight offices to get their right back.

The article mentions the detention of more than two thousand people in Delhi on 10 October, the blocked roads, and the metro stations shut before the march to the Supreme Court on 12 October. The writer says that when the issue is the honesty of elections, arresting protesters and journalists is even more worrying. A confident government would answer questions openly, because police force cannot change public feeling.

Khan also raises the impact on minorities. The opposition and activists allege that the revision has hit Muslims and other minorities harder. The vote of more than twenty crore (200 million) Indian Muslims cannot depend on religion or on the government's convenience. He demands that the government say whose name was removed and why, and how many were restored, and that international monitoring bodies examine these figures.

The writer concludes that these young people do not want to abandon democracy but to strengthen it. If the process is truly fair, why does the government not answer its critics with evidence? Democracy is made not by population, growth rate or the number of elections, but by the freedom to challenge power and by independent institutions.
nazar: This article is an outside view, and that is why it matters. The claim of being the largest democracy is made to the world again and again, and now the world is weighing Delhi's barricades against that very claim.

Who should bear the burden of proof is the real question in this whole dispute. The article says so directly, though it has taken most of its figures from media reports, not from its own investigation.
sawal: Who must prove why a name was cut, the Commission or the voter?
ref: Article 326
The provision of the Constitution that gives every citizen over 18 the right to vote, unless disqualified under the law.

h: Protest needs a shared strategy, not scattered events
dek: A Siasat editorial says that since the government is bent on suppressing protest at any cost, those fighting for democratic rights must plan together, not separately, and within the law.
body: This Siasat editorial was written on the day of the Tiranga March (national flag march), and it opens with an accusation: the central government has decided to crush the protests against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. According to the paper, those who announce protests are being detained even though they gave advance notice, and court directions are being ignored.

The article says that over the past week force was used again and again, student leaders and young people were held at police stations, and lawyers, journalists and members of civil society were treated the same way as students. The editorial calls it deeply regrettable that the government is relying only on the police to silence democratic voices.

The paper describes the Cockroach Janata Party's Tiranga March as a fully peaceful event in which students and young people wanted to register their protest carrying the national flag. According to the article, the Modi government was uneasy about this march. The march was stopped, Abhijeet Dipke was detained, Neha Bora was arrested and there were attempts to disperse the crowd.

This is where the editorial comes to its real point. If the government is set on suppressing protest at any cost, then protesters must replace scattered events with a shared, broad strategy: consult like-minded people, organisations and unions, explore legal options, and stay within the law and the Constitution with a plan that gives the government or the police no chance to crush them.

The final warning reaches far. According to the editorial, if democratic and constitutional rights are not protected today, rights will keep being cut in the future, and the biggest losers will be the poor and the marginalised, who will slowly be made second-class citizens.
nazar: This editorial goes beyond anger and asks the movement a hard question: can protests scattered under different banners stand up to a government that is ready every day with a new restriction? Discipline and unity in the face of force, that is its prescription.

The warning about second-class citizenship links this movement to the question of equality, beyond the voter rolls. Those whose names are cut are often the very people whose voices are already the weakest.
sawal: Can scattered protest take on organised power?
ref: Jantar Mantar
Delhi's traditional protest site near Parliament. In October 2026 the government removed it from the list of protest sites, citing Parliament's security.

h: Welcoming Min Aung Hlaing: Malaysia's double standard on justice
dek: Aizat Shamsuddin's sharp comment on the Putrajaya visit of Myanmar's coup general and the return of refugees.
body: On 8 October, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim hosted Myanmar's President Min Aung Hlaing in Putrajaya. It was his first visit to Malaysia since the 2021 coup. Nine days earlier, Malaysia had sent 1,476 Myanmar nationals back by sea, the first phase of a plan to return 5,000 people. According to Aizat Shamsuddin, executive director of Initiate.my, this pragmatic diplomacy gives a middle power standing in the eyes of a United States that is retreating from accountability.

Since May, anti-Rohingya hate and false news have spread fast. By the end of July, at least nine Rohingya community schools had closed or faced closure orders, and more than a hundred Rohingya were driven out of a village in Penang. Yet according to the police, their share in crime is just 0.02 percent. After losing state elections, the government wants to look tough.

The question of double standards is the sharpest. In November 2024, Anwar supported the ICC warrant against Netanyahu, and that same month the ICC prosecutor sought a warrant for Min Aung Hlaing. The 2016-17 campaign under his command drove more than seven lakh (700,000) Rohingya into Bangladesh. The writer says a peacemaker's credibility comes from applying the same standard to everyone.

The UN refugee agency was not involved in this return, so it is not certain that people went back of their own free will. Those sent back reportedly included 27 children. War continues in Rakhine, and a day before the returns began, there were reports that at least 50 civilians had been killed in a military air strike.

Malaysia's frustration over sharing the burden is fair, but according to the writer it is no excuse for returns without protection. He demands that Myanmar's return to ASEAN be tied to real progress on the Five-Point Consensus, and that returns be halted until there is an independent investigation.
nazar: This article is a picture of a time when international courts are under pressure from all sides, and every new welcome makes the next one easier. Mongolia invited Putin, Hungary invited Netanyahu, and now Malaysia has invited a general whose campaign is the subject of a genocide case in an international court. The heaviest price is paid by the Rohingya, who have neither a country nor a hearing.
sawal: Should the measure of justice change depending on whether someone is a friend or a foe?
ref: Five-Point Consensus
An agreement between ASEAN and Myanmar's military after the 2021 coup, which spoke of ending violence and holding inclusive talks. The military did not implement it.
Non-refoulement
The principle of international law that a refugee cannot be sent back to a place where their life or freedom is in danger.

h: Yemen is calling again, but Turkey does not need to go back
dek: Historian Oğul Tuna's warning on the Mecca agreement between Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan: this is someone else's war.
body: In Turkey's popular memory, Yemen is recorded as a deep wound. Folk songs are still sung about the soldiers from Anatolia who were sent there and never came back. Writing in Jacobin, historian Oğul Tuna says the glory of empire went to the state, while the deaths went to ordinary families. After 1869 the Ottoman government tried to tighten its grip on Yemen, but the memoirs of Ahmed Muhtar Pasha show that its control stayed limited to the towns and revolts kept flaring up.

According to the writer, the 2015 Saudi attack repeated the same lesson. Despite help from the US and Western powers, Saudi Arabia could not defeat the Houthi movement, Ansar Allah. The result was a humanitarian disaster, and the profits went to arms companies. According to Tuna, the Houthis are not progressive, but military superiority could not shape Yemen.

Now, on 7 August, Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed the Mecca agreement, under which an attack on one member will be treated as an attack on all. Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan compared it to NATO's Article 5. On 5 October the three agreed to activate collective deterrence. Ankara is considering air defence support, and on 13 October Trump spoke of asking Erdoğan for help against the Houthis.

The writer argues that this agreement could serve a US-led regional order in which Israel clashes with Iran and America's allies expand their reach. Turkey has not been the target of any Houthi attack, yet like Saudi Arabia, it is being drawn into someone else's war.

According to Tuna, those in power call their strategic interests the national interest, and then ask ordinary people to die for it. The profit goes to defence companies, the price is paid by soldiers and Yemeni civilians. His conclusion is clear: Turkey does not need to return to Yemen.
nazar: This article reminds us that the account of war is written not in maps and agreements but in the homes from which sons are sent away. A military alliance of three countries is one more threat to the people of Yemen, who are already devastated. The memory kept alive in folk songs tells more truth than official statements.
sawal: In the name of national interest, who gives their life and who reaps the profit?
ref: Mecca agreement
A collective defence pact signed on 7 August 2026 between Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, under which an attack on one is treated as an attack on all.
Ansar Allah
Yemen's Houthi movement, which controls a large part of northern Yemen, including the capital Sanaa.

h: Chandra Thapa: Nepal is raising its daughters to be unpaid workers
dek: If housework were given a value, a Nepali woman's yearly labour would be worth more than the per capita income, yet less is spent on daughters' education.
body: Chandra Thapa, a professor of finance at Strathclyde Business School, points out that the 2017-18 Labour Force Survey recorded women's labour force participation in Nepal at 26.3 percent and men's at 53.8 percent. In his view, this figure counts only work that earns a wage or a profit. Cooking, carrying water, caring for children and the elderly, growing grain in the fields: all of it is left out of the count.

By an International Labour Organization estimate, unpaid care work in 64 countries equals nine percent of the world's output, and women put in three quarters of its hours. A 2022 study of 3,500 households in Nepal's Bagmati and Madhesh provinces found that women spend about six hours a day on housework and care, and men two and a quarter hours.

Thapa calculates its value at the minimum wage of 101 rupees an hour, in force since July 2025. About 2,190 hours a year comes to nearly 2.21 lakh rupees, and adding one extra hour of work such as settling quarrels at home brings it to about 2.6 lakh rupees, roughly 1,900 dollars. That is more than Nepal's per capita GDP in 2024, which was 1,447 dollars. The writer considers this a minimum estimate.

The writer argues that families invest where they expect a return, and a daughter's return is hidden twice over. Her work at home is not counted, and her work outside pays less. Citing a 2018 study by Shaleen Khanal, he says that in both villages and cities more is spent on sons' education and they are sent to private schools more often. In the 2021 census, male literacy is 83.6 percent and female literacy 69.4 percent.

Based on the World Bank's gender employment gap index, Thapa estimates that Nepal's gap of about 34 percent costs 9 to 15 billion dollars in output every year, and if even a third of it is linked to education, the loss is 3 to 5 billion dollars a year. He makes three demands: that the National Statistics Office publish the value of household work every year alongside GDP, that the government give private school enrolment figures by gender, and that girls get scholarships at the secondary level.
nazar: This article puts injustice inside the home in the language of economics, and that is its strength. Equal enrolment figures often offer comfort, but Thapa shows that equal enrolment is not equal spending. The same story repeats in India's villages, where a sister leaves school so her brother's fees can be paid.
sawal: If housework is not even counted, how do we measure equality?
ref: Labour force participation rate
The share of the working-age population that is working or looking for work. Unpaid housework is usually not counted in it.

h: Shehzad Sharjeel: We all killed Laiba
dek: According to the Pakistani satirist, the death of a promising young woman is the crime not of one accused man but of the whole society and a failed state.
body: Poet and satirist Shehzad Sharjeel hopes the accused in Laiba's case will be arrested and put on trial. But his real argument is that the verdict should go against society, because all of us together killed Laiba. According to the writer, so much money was extorted from her family in the name of a job for her brother or admission to a foreign university that the family sold off its life's savings.

Laiba was a gold medallist from a well-known university. The writer asks: if scholarships are meant to remove obstacles, why must people pay brokers posing as advisers to get them? He says that universities and the whole education system teach neither the skills to live life nor the habit of thinking and questioning, and that a state that fails its citizens is safe for no one, whether for life, dignity or investment.

Sharjeel says young people ask him for jobs every week, though he has no connections and a bribe is expected everywhere. He bitterly suggests that it would be better to use the bribe money to set up a roadside food cart.

A large part of the article is about the condition of women. According to the writer, women face a greater risk of sexual violence and are expected to stay silent for the sake of family honour. This mindset shows up in homes, at rallies and on television. He criticises a former military dictator who defended an accused man on TV, and also a popular leader who linked women's clothing to men's behaviour. In a viral clip, a man linked to the PPP is seen saying that if they like a woman, they carry her off, and he is still in his party.

The Prime Minister has ordered the police chief and the interior minister to arrest the man whose actions led to Laiba's death. The writer jokes that the cabinet probably spent the rest of the day thinking about how to make Pakistan look attractive for investment, while visiting cricketers get royal security and ordinary citizens stay unsafe.
nazar: Sharjeel's anger starts with one death and reaches the whole system: brokers, bribes, unemployment and the pressure on women to stay silent. It is a restless, scattered piece, but its restlessness is its truth. In India too, the stories of families cheated in the name of exams, admissions and jobs are no different.
sawal: Will the accused alone answer for Laiba's death, or society too?
ref: PPP
Pakistan Peoples Party, the party founded by Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, with particular influence in Sindh.

h: Komal Rajak: It is unemployment, not the 'Gen Z' label, that explains young people's anger
dek: Calling the movement against the NEET paper leak a generational mood distracts from the real questions; according to the writer, only the medium of protest has changed.
body: Komal Rajak disagrees that the recent protests should simply be called a 'Gen Z' uprising. In her view, a generation's name tells us when the protesters were born, not why they protested. Youth movements are not new; she recalls Bhagat Singh's Naujawan Bharat Sabha (Youth Society of India), founded in 1926.

The article examines the 2026 NEET movement. There were protests over paper leaks in 2024 too, but this time it became a mass movement. According to the writer, the spark was a remark by Chief Justice Surya Kant comparing unemployed young people active in media and RTI (right to information) to cockroaches. A later clarification did not help. A satirical account called 'Cockroach Janata Party' reached more than 1.9 crore (19 million) people on Instagram in a week, thousands marched towards Sansad Marg, and in the end a Union minister had to resign.

Drawing on sociologist Karl Mannheim, Rajak says that people read the same historical experience differently according to caste, class, gender, religion and employment. According to Doug McAdam, students and the unemployed are seen more in such protests because the cost of taking part is lower for them.

Throughout history young people's energy has been present in every era; only its tools have changed. The Naujawan Bharat Sabha had printing presses and meetings, JP's Total Revolution movement had radio and newspapers, the 2011 Anna movement had 24-hour TV and Facebook, and the 2019 protest against the 13-point roster had hashtags. The writer reminds us that the same energy was there in the 1990 anti-Mandal protests and in the 1927 Mahad Satyagraha, which means young people are themselves divided by caste and class.

Her conclusion is that this movement was not a revolution. It was built by graduate unemployment, the falling credibility of exams, the court's remark and new structures of communication, all together. According to the article, 67 percent of the unemployed aged 20 to 29 are graduates. Memes, short videos and AI-made images sped up the turning of anger into participation, and the writer calls this an ecological shift in how movements are organised.
nazar: This article points at the media habit of folding every protest into memes and style. The generation label is easy, because it pushes aside uncomfortable questions like unemployment and exam scams. Written from a Bahujan (marginalised-caste) perspective, it is also an important reminder that young people are not all the same, and their circumstances decide which way their energy will go.
sawal: When protest is given a generation's name, whose questions get buried?
ref: Biographical availability
Sociologist Doug McAdam's idea that people with fewer family or job responsibilities are more likely to join risky movements.
13-point roster
A system of applying reservation in universities by treating each department as a unit, which led to large protests in 2019.

h: OpenAI's outcry over spying, and its silence over its own theft
dek: Belén Fernández's sardonic question about turning one engineer's arrest into a national security crisis.
body: On 9 October the FBI arrested Abdulrahman Alfauzan, a 35-year-old Saudi engineer working at OpenAI. The US Justice Department alleges that he hid a sound-recording device in a conference room at the company's San Francisco office. According to Gizmodo, such a device sells online for about 14 dollars.

Al Jazeera columnist Belén Fernández asks why this case is being presented like Cold War espionage. From the US intelligence chief to the FBI director and the Attorney General, everyone called it a matter of the race for superintelligence and of national security. According to the writer, this shows that the wall between corporations and government in the US has collapsed.

The irony is that OpenAI itself faces charges of using other people's work. On 8 October several newspapers, including USA Today, filed a suit in the federal court in Manhattan alleging that millions of their articles were used without permission to train ChatGPT. In July the New York Times had accused the company of destroying evidence. The writer says that when the company does this, it is called the good of humanity, while an accusation against one person becomes a national crisis.

Fernández turns to the bigger picture. AI companies make profits by taking away jobs and are tied to mass surveillance. Federal agencies buy people's personal data from tech companies. Against this, the sudden concern about spying seems suspicious to her.

The writer alleges that companies like OpenAI that win Pentagon contracts are partners in US military actions in Venezuela and Iran. She cites an AP report that US tech companies helped Israel find targets faster in Gaza and Lebanon, while civilian deaths kept rising.
nazar: This article uses satire to make a serious point: when tech companies and the government start speaking the same language, security comes to mean protecting the company's secrets, not ordinary people's lives and privacy. The debate over the accountability of those who build technology that picks targets on the battlefield is still to come.
sawal: Whom does national security protect, the company or the citizen?
ref: Superintelligence
The idea of artificial intelligence that surpasses human intelligence. According to the article, the Trump administration has begun using this term for AI.

h: A history-sheeter's life is just as precious: no bail for three policemen in custodial death case
dek: The Orissa High Court said the right to life under Article 21 does not depend on a person's past record or social standing.
body: On 14 October the Orissa High Court rejected the bail pleas of a sub-inspector, an assistant sub-inspector and a constable. The three are accused of a man's death in the Koraput area in 2017 and have been in custody since 29 August 2025. Justice V. Narasingh delivered the ruling.

The case goes back to 30 January 2017, when these policemen went to catch a man linked to fourteen cases. The official story was that he fell on Canal Road while fleeing on a motorcycle, was injured and died in hospital. The dead man's mother approached the Human Rights Commission and the High Court, after which the CID-CB (Crime Branch) took over the investigation and an FIR was registered under several sections, including murder.

The defence said the death was an accident. But according to witness statements, the police first hit him with a pipe, which made him fall, then beat him further and took him away in a jeep. The court noted that there were twenty-four injuries on the dead man's body and that several medical opinions had been sought so that the death could be shown as an accident. The court also took into account the risk of pressure on witnesses.

The court said clearly that the label of history-sheeter (a person with a police record) does not reduce the protection of anyone's life, and that the police exist to guard citizens' lives. The accused can apply for bail again after the key witnesses have testified.
nazar: In custodial death cases, the dead person's criminal record often becomes the defence. This ruling rejects that argument outright. But it is also worth noting that it took eight years and a mother's long fight for one death's investigation to reach an FIR.
sawal: Can an accused person's record become an excuse for police violence?
ref: Article 21
The article of the Constitution that gives every person the right to life and personal liberty. It cannot be taken away without due process of law.

h: Bookstalls targeted in Bengal as Left parties' stalls come under attack
dek: Left bookstalls set up during Durga Puja were smashed in several places, including Dhakuria in Kolkata, and the High Court said the opposition's voice cannot be silenced like this.
body: Since 1954, Left parties in Bengal have set up bookstalls during the festival season. According to an Alt News report, this year these stalls have become the centre of a political clash. On 10 September, Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari told puja committees that if the CPI(M) used the word Sharadotsav instead of Durga Puja, it should not be given space for a stall.

On the evening of 14 October, CPI(ML) Liberation workers were putting up a stall near the Dhakuria bus stand when ten or twelve men who said they were from the BJP-RSS arrived and told them to clear the spot. Manas Chatterjee of Liberation alleges that he was grabbed and beaten, and that the police left as soon as the beating began. Amalendu Bhushan Chowdhury, an 89-year-old worker who came to his rescue, was also allegedly beaten, and Achyut Chakraborty of the CPI(M) says hot tea was thrown at him.

The police say the required permission for the stall had not been taken. The Left parties reply that the land belongs to the municipal corporation, the fee had been paid, and for fifty years the practice has simply been to inform the local police station. Similar incidents have been reported from Behala, Kasba, Shibpur and Naihati.

Meanwhile, Justice Saugata Bhattacharyya of the Calcutta High Court, hearing a case from Bongaon, questioned the government's selective permissions and said the opposition's voice should not be suppressed this way. On Thursday he allowed the CPI(M) to set up a stall within a hundred metres of the chosen spot and placed the responsibility for security on police officers.
nazar: It is hard to see how a bookstall threatens the devotion of a puja pandal. When those in power begin deciding, in the name of a festival, which ideas may reach the crowds, the attack is not just on one party. It is on Bengal's old tradition of reading and argument.
sawal: Since when did selling books at a festival become a threat?
ref: Sharadotsav
The festival of autumn, an old Bengali word used for Durga Puja.

h: Backward class status does not travel with a change of religion: Supreme Court keeps Tamil Nadu order struck down
dek: The court held unconstitutional a government order that gave Muslim backward class certificates to backward class and Dalit people who embraced Islam.
body: On 15 October, a Supreme Court bench of Justice Prashant Kumar Mishra and Justice Sri Chandrashekhar dismissed the Tamil Nadu government's appeal. This upheld the Madras High Court ruling that had struck down Government Order No. 314 of March 2024. Under that order, people who converted to Islam from Backward, Most Backward, Denotified or Scheduled Caste communities could get a certificate for one of seven notified Muslim backward communities, opening the way to 3.5 percent reservation.

The case is that of Sameer Ahmed, formerly named Paramasivara, who embraced Islam in 2015. In 2020 the tehsil (local revenue) office refused him a Muslim Labbai certificate, saying he had changed his religion, not his caste. The High Court declared the order unconstitutional on the same ground.

The Supreme Court said reservation is not a personal thing that a person carries along, but is tied to a class recognised in the Constitution. Backwardness suffered in Hindu society cannot be carried into another religion to create backward class status there. According to the court, the order did not explain how people from different groups would be counted in those same seven communities, and a jamaat (community body) certificate can only confirm a conversion, not decide backward status.

The court did mention groups within Muslim society such as the Ashraf, Ajlaf and Arzal, but said they do not form a uniform caste structure. After the verdict, M.K. Stalin has asked the state government to file a review petition.
nazar: The court accepts that Muslim society has divisions like Ashraf and Arzal, yet says a convert does not carry his social burden with him. On the ground, caste does not vanish with a change of religion; the Pasmanda movement has been saying this for decades. The question is when the law's definitions will match this reality.
sawal: Does changing religion lift the burden of caste?
ref: Constitution (Scheduled Castes) Order, 1950
Its third paragraph limits Scheduled Caste status to those who follow Hinduism, Sikhism and Buddhism.

h: Never counted, now being erased: Delhi's Gadia Lohars in the SIR
dek: Most voters of this nomadic blacksmith community, who live in tents by the roadside, have received notices because they have no papers from before 2002.
body: During the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of Delhi's electoral rolls, Behanbox looked at the condition of the Gadia Lohars, blacksmiths who once travelled in bullock carts and now live in roadside tents and shanties on the city's edges. According to the report, in the Patthar Market area of Mangolpuri, 38 of the 45 voters at one booth got notices saying they were unmapped. Matra, who is over sixty, says she was told at the office that people who live on the road cannot get a voter card.

In Sagarpur, all 55 voters at the booth of brothers Jitendra and Jagdish received notices. They submitted PAN, Aadhaar, ration cards and electricity bills, but the BLO (booth level officer) asked for their parents' papers. All they have from before 2002 is a 1990 DUSIB survey, which is not clearly included in the government's indicative list. In Dwarka Sector 3, Savitri says her shanty has been demolished about fifty times, and she lost her 2002 voter card in one such drive.

According to a 2019 survey, only two percent of people in these settlements had a caste certificate, while almost all had Aadhaar, which is not accepted as proof on its own. The 34 shop-cum-houses built under a 2003 rehabilitation scheme have still not been allotted, and people say one reason was that they did not have voter cards.

Activist Deepa Pawar traces the roots of this stigma to the Criminal Tribes Act of 1871. The community is asking for a separate column in the 2027 Census, but there has been no reply from the government.
nazar: Asking people whose homes have been torn down again and again for an unbroken trail of papers is a cruel irony. If, in the name of cleaning the rolls, the first to be pushed out are those without a fixed address, then this process is making democracy smaller.
sawal: If your home has been broken fifty times, where do you find old papers?
ref: Denotified tribes
Communities that a British-era law of 1871 declared criminal by birth. The law was repealed in 1952, but the stigma remained.

h: Committee formed, but sugarcane farmers stand firm: protest to go on until prices are fixed
dek: Karnataka's sugarcane farmers welcomed the Centre's four-member committee, but said they will not end their sit-in until new prices for sugar and sugarcane are announced.
body: Karnataka's sugarcane farmers want the minimum selling price of sugar raised to Rs 60 a kilo, and the fair and remunerative price of sugarcane raised from Rs 3,650 to Rs 5,500 a tonne. They also want transparency in weighing and in the assessment of recovery at factories, computerised weighbridges, and a law that makes farmers stakeholders in sugar mills, with a share in the profits from by-products such as molasses, ethanol and electricity.

The central government has set up a committee led by agricultural scientist Ramesh Chand. On 15 October near Belagavi, Chunnappa Pujeri of the Karnataka Rajya Raitha Sangha and Hasiru Sene said it was good that all sides were represented on the committee, but it was no reason to call off the protest. Shashikant Padasalagi proposed separate sugar prices for household and industrial use, just as domestic and commercial gas cylinders are priced differently.

After a meeting with Union ministers in Delhi on 12 October, state Cooperation Minister Laxman Savadi said Shivraj Singh Chouhan and Pralhad Joshi had come unprepared and the officials showed no urgency. The Centre proposes that the committee give its recommendations in about a month, after which a decision on prices will be taken.

On 14 October, a sit-in at the Kognoli toll plaza on the Mumbai-Bengaluru National Highway 48 brought traffic to a halt. Raju Shetti from Maharashtra said members of his organisation would join the Hubballi Chalo padyatra (protest march on foot).
nazar: Forming a committee is an old government trick that puts anger off for a few weeks. The farmers' real demand goes beyond price: they want a share in the whole income of the sugar industry, which is an invitation to rethink the relationship between the field and the factory.
sawal: Why shouldn't the person who grows the cane get a share of the mill's profit?
ref: FRP
Fair and remunerative price, the minimum price that sugar mills must pay sugarcane farmers. It is fixed by the central government.

h: Ankita Bhandari's parents detained at India Gate before dawn
dek: The family was demanding that Dushyant Kumar Gautam's appointment as governor be put on hold until the CBI finishes its probe into the allegations about a VIP.
body: The parents of Ankita Bhandari, the 19-year-old receptionist killed in Uttarakhand in September 2022, sat in protest at India Gate through the night. According to Sabrang's report, Delhi Police detained them at about 3:45 am on 15 October and released them around 5 am. Several Congress leaders who had joined the protest were also detained.

The family wants BJP leader Dushyant Kumar Gautam's appointment as Governor of Sikkim, announced on 12 October, put on hold until the CBI completes its probe into whether a VIP had a hand in the murder. Her father, Virendra Bhandari, gave the government a 24-hour ultimatum, and her mother, Soni Devi, appealed to the President to step in. The family wants the probe monitored by a Supreme Court judge and access to call records. It does not question the convictions of the three people already sentenced.

In May 2025, a court sentenced resort owner Pulkit Arya and two employees to life imprisonment. It is alleged that Ankita was pressured to provide "extra services" to a guest, which she refused. A recording that surfaced in December 2025 named Gautam.

Gautam denies any role and has taken defamation action. He is not an accused in the murder case, and the earlier SIT (special investigation team) had said it found no evidence that any senior leader was involved. On the recommendation of Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami, the CBI has registered a case against an unknown person.
nazar: Picking up elderly parents who are seeking justice for their daughter before the sun is up shows how uneasy power is with questions. Holding back an appointment while a probe is on does not declare anyone guilty. It is the minimum needed to protect public trust.
sawal: If the probe is unfinished, why the hurry for a high office?
ref: Ankita Bhandari case
The murder in September 2022 of an employee of the Vanantara resort near Rishikesh. Her body was found in the Chilla canal.

h: A dream of the deep sea, fishers sinking in debt
dek: A Mongabay India investigation finds that of 392 deep-sea fishing vessels sanctioned under the Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada Yojana, only 131 had been ordered by September 2026, and early beneficiaries are struggling with debt and faulty boats.
body: Shaju Antony, a traditional fisher from Kerala, applied to the government scheme in 2020 at his priest's suggestion. He raised about Rs 72 lakh for his share, got the boat in December 2023, and then the breakdowns began. Repairs cost another Rs 30 lakh. He knocked on the state government's doors for months and finally gave up. His question is simple: why were fishers not consulted when boats were being built for them?

The first story in this series by Mongabay India and the Pulitzer Center examines the deep-sea vessel scheme launched in 2020 under the Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada Yojana. Overfishing, erosion and development pressure along the coasts pushed the government towards deeper waters, for costly fish such as tuna, shark and squid. Under the scheme, the fisher pays 60 percent of the boat's cost, which comes to at least Rs 1.25 crore, and the government pays 40 percent. Nets and other gear are not included.

According to RTI replies and state data, of the 392 boats sanctioned for 2020-25, only 131 had been ordered by September 2026. Karnataka and Maharashtra lead; Andhra and Kerala have only six boats each in operation, while Odisha, Gujarat, Goa and Tamil Nadu found no takers. In Kerala, the boats built by Cochin Shipyard have complaints about compressors, engines and leaks. No owner is making a profit, and together they owe more than Rs 4 crore.

Kiran Koli, a union leader in Maharashtra, applied under the older Blue Revolution scheme in 2017-18 and got his boat in June 2026, nearly ten years later, and the last two instalments of the subsidy are still pending. Tamil Nadu's fishers stayed away after seeing low catches and a lack of training; those in Gujarat cite the absence of tax relief on diesel. According to the report, the fisheries department did not answer Mongabay's questions.
nazar: The scheme promises to turn the small fisher into a big entrepreneur, but places a risk worth crores on his head alone. When his opinion is not sought in building the boat and the subsidy is stuck for years, the burden of development falls on the very people in whose name the scheme was made. Without the voices of coastal settlements, the dream of a blue economy will float only on paper.
sawal: Who builds a boat for a fisher without asking the fisher?
ref: Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada Yojana
A central scheme launched in 2020 to raise fish production, exports and fishers' incomes. Subsidy for deep-sea vessels is one part of it.
Blue Revolution
An older central mission to promote fish farming and marine fishing, later folded into the Matsya Sampada Yojana.

h: Lost in the desert: an old man who searches for those who cross the border
dek: This film in Al Jazeera's Witness series follows Rafael Laraenza, who searches for missing migrants in the desert on the US-Mexico border, as he sets out to find a mother's missing son.
body: On 27 September, Witness, Al Jazeera English's documentary series, showed filmmaker Vincent DeLuca's film Finding Desert Angels. Its subject is the region where the US-Mexico border runs through the desert, where every year many people set out on foot in search of a better life and never return.

At the centre of the film is Rafael Laraenza, regarded as a pioneer of search and rescue work. According to the film's introduction, for twenty-five years he has been the man families call when no one else will help. His work is not part of any government department. It is a risky effort he runs on his own, with very few resources, where someone's life is at stake.

Now Laraenza is getting old and his health is failing. In this state, a mother comes to him whose son went missing after crossing the border. The film follows this search, where every minute counts, because in the desert, lack of water, the heat and losing the way can kill within a few days.

DeLuca's camera takes him into a harsh landscape that few people ever see, and from which some never come out. According to the film's introduction, Laraenza puts his own life at risk in this search. It is less a story of adventure and more a story of the silence that falls to the families of the missing.

The background is this: over the past three decades, the US built tight surveillance and walls along the border near cities, pushing those who cross towards longer and more dangerous desert routes. Human rights groups, and US government figures themselves, show that thousands of people have died on these routes, and many bodies are never identified.

So the burden of finding the missing often falls on volunteers and families. Through one man's persistence, the film shows who is left responsible for a person's search, identity and family's grief when the state sees that person only as an illegal entry.
nazar: This story seems far away, but it is not. Thousands of young men from Punjab, Haryana and Gujarat reach this very border by 'donkey' routes, and many of their families too are waiting for a call from someone like Laraenza. A policy that treats migration as a crime does not stop deaths; it only pushes them out of sight into the desert.
That a sick old man is doing, on his own, the work governments should be doing is the biggest question this film raises.
sawal: Whose job is it to find someone lost at the border?
ref: Witness
Al Jazeera English's long-running documentary series, in which independent filmmakers from around the world make films about ordinary people's lives.
Donkey route
A way of reaching the US or Europe through several countries by illegal and dangerous routes. Many people from India, especially Punjab and Gujarat, pay agents huge sums to make this journey.

h: The golden cage of fame, where the singer is left alone
dek: A long essay by Dipti Kushwah on Sammukh: from Kurt Cobain to Sulli, how fame becomes a prison in the lives of popular music stars.
body: The essay opens with a concert scene. The singer is on stage, a roaring crowd in front, his name everywhere. Then the lights go out, people go home, and the singer too goes home alone. For Dipti Kushwah, this return is the saddest truth of fame: the songs that comforted strangers could not bring peace to the person who made them.

The writer lays out a long list: Kurt Cobain, Chris Cornell, Chester Bennington, Avicii, Amy Winehouse, Jonghyun, Sulli, Goo Hara, Michael Jackson, Freddie Mercury and Whitney Houston. She says clearly that they died of different causes: depression, addiction, illness, brutal tours, invasion of privacy. The common thread is not death, but that inside fame a person is slowly evicted from their own life.

Her argument is that the image built for the audience becomes bigger than the human being, and the market wants novelty that does not break with past success. Cobain's rebellion became a saleable style after 'Nevermind'. Avicii played more than 250 shows a year, retired at 26 and died at 28. The writer rejects outright the myth of the 'tortured genius'.

Women are hit differently. They are always expected to stay young, beautiful and marketable. Amy Winehouse's talent was buried under tabloid spectacle. The writer links the deaths of Sulli and Goo Hara, caught between South Korea's idol system and online abuse, to patriarchy and the unchecked internet mob.

In the end the essay asks for compassion instead of sensation: music companies, managers, platforms and listeners should give artists rest, mental health support and the freedom to step back. It comes with a list of ten sources, including the World Health Organization's guidelines on reporting suicide.
nazar: It is rare to see an essay in Hindi on popular music written with such seriousness and detail. Its strength is its restraint: not every death is tied into one story, and the blame is not put on any one party. The question is also for listeners, who find sadness beautiful in a song and a burden in life.
sawal: Do we love an artist only after they are gone?
ref: Idol system

The system in South Korea's entertainment industry in which artists are trained for years, then shaped and sold.
According to the writer, private life and fans' expectations get mixed up in it.

h: Jantar Mantar's cockroaches at a New York dinner
dek: Amitava Kumar's Substack essay, in Aditya Shukla's translation on Sammukh: an evening at a fundraiser, and the struggle rising on Delhi's streets.
body: The well-known English writer Amitava Kumar first wrote this essay on Substack. Sammukh has published it in its new series in Aditya Shukla's translation. The title is Sangharsh ki zaroorat (The need for struggle), and the subtitle inside speaks of celebrating the cockroach.

It begins on an evening in New York. It was a fundraising dinner for the Asian American Writers' Workshop, which also opened the Diwali celebrations. According to the writer, Salman Rushdie said there that India is boiling and its young people have given a rare moment of hope after a long time. Rushdie also recalled the festivals of his Bombay childhood that belonged to everyone, beyond religion.

That same evening, filmmaker Mira Nair's birthday was celebrated. The writer says Nair expressed pride in the cockroaches fighting for democracy and called herself a cockroach mom. Amitava links this to historian Mukul Kesavan's remark that Jantar Mantar may have raised a whole generation of desi young people like Zohran Mamdani.

Then the tone sharpens. The writer expresses anger at police brutality and attacks on journalists in Delhi and says that in the country that calls itself the mother of democracy, democracy is being killed on the streets of its capital. Citing an article by Nidhi Suresh, he quotes activist Neha Bora, who mentions Hathras, Unnao and mob lynchings and asks: when people are being killed simply for existing, what choice is there but to take to the streets?

At the end, Amitava draws a picture of struggle rising on many fronts at once: the energy of the street against power, and young people organising against crony capitalism. For him this is a fight for a new understanding of how to live, standing up to tired historical clichés.
nazar: This essay is not a report but something like a writer's diary, where the glitter of the diaspora literary world and the wounds of Delhi's streets share a single page. Its honesty lies in refusing to hide this contradiction. The translation brings it to the Hindi reader with the same restlessness.
sawal: Does the hope of a writer far away reach the street?
ref: Asian American Writers' Workshop

A non-profit literary organisation in New York that gives a platform to American writers of Asian origin.
This essay begins at its fundraising event.

h: Set Dostoevsky free from the quotation market
dek: Nishant Kaushik's essay on Hindwi Bela: how, in the age of social media, Dostoevsky and existentialism became decorative quotes.
body: In this instalment of the Jagah-Jagah 2.0 (Here and There 2.0) series, Nishant Kaushik begins with an honest admission: many readers find Dostoevsky tiresome. The prose is dense, the sentences long, the details dry, and the books are full of dreams, taverns and letter-like monologues. Still, the writer considers him great, because he made the novel a place to examine a godless society, a critique of the Enlightenment and the turmoil of the modern mind.

According to the writer, new translations have come out recently and 'White Nights' has been widely read, but this is no assurance of deep engagement. Dostoevsky is now part of the crowd, with Kafka, Kierkegaard, Nietzsche, Camus, Jaun Elia, Sylvia Plath and Bukowski, whose lines are repeated to decorate self-absorption.

The second part brings in Jordan Peterson, who took over YouTube around 2016-17. Peterson, who wrote the foreword to Solzhenitsyn's 'The Gulag Archipelago', called the hero of 'Crime and Punishment' a man of the post-religious world. Nishant sees this as a simplified pull towards religious revival, one that appealed to the American right.

The third part is about the shallow revival of existentialism. Sisyphus, Meursault and Gregor Samsa are now less literature and more mood signals. The writer accepts that poverty, unemployment and inequality are real, but says this popularity is more a habit of consumption than a taste for reading, where books, reels and quotes are packaged and served.

The writer points out that Tolstoy's 'Confession' and 'Resurrection' present life's crisis more clearly and readably, but are not trending. He ends with a satirical passage from an old diary of his, about people who photograph books and act out boredom.
nazar: The essay does not scold the reader; it holds up a mirror. Its complaint is not with Dostoevsky's admirers but with the market that, as with Ghalib and Gulzar, reduces every great writer to a single line. After reading it, you want to drop the quotes and pick up the whole novel.
sawal: Can reading quotes take the place of reading a book?
ref: Novel of ideas

A novel in which characters and events become the medium for philosophical, moral or political debate.
The writer counts Dostoevsky among the founders of this form.

h: Devika Rani's hesitation and Himanshu Rai's resolve
dek: Anirudh Sharma in Sammukh's column Ilmi-Filmi: how one love opened the door of Indian cinema to educated women.
body: Anirudh Sharma begins this instalment of his column Ilmi-Filmi with a remark about love. People in love sometimes do things they never meant to, and those things leave an impact like cutting through a mountain to change a river's course. According to the writer, the story of Himanshu Rai and Devika Rani is one of these.

Himanshu Rai made his first film, 'The Light of Asia', in 1925, and it was widely praised in England. Around that time he met Devika Rani, who was nearly half his age. The two were drawn to each other, but nothing came of it. Later Himanshu wanted Devika to act in his next film, 'Shiraz'.

The obstacle was Devika's background. She came from an educated, respected family with ties to Rabindranath Tagore. In those days acting in films was considered deeply disgraceful, and mostly poor or uneducated women took it up. After much agonising, Devika said no.

Himanshu decided he would bring educated women from good families onto the screen. He chose Enakshi Rama Rau for the lead role in 'Shiraz'. The film won even more praise and Enakshi became famous as the first highly educated actress. According to the writer, this stung Devika, because the honour could have been hers.

The writer believes Himanshu's resolve changed the film world. The way opened for women who had stayed away out of fear, and in the end Devika too made up her mind. The rest of the story, love, marriage, the rise and fall of Bombay Talkies and the breakdown of the relationship, the writer leaves for later instalments.
nazar: This short piece, told in a storyteller's style, lifts film history above gossip and makes it a story of social change. It also brings back a forgotten name like Enakshi Rama Rau. The writer is a filmmaker himself, so he understands both the hesitation and the resolve behind the screen.
sawal: Whose resolve opened the way for women in cinema?
ref: Bombay Talkies

The film studio started in 1934 by Himanshu Rai and Devika Rani.
It gave Hindi cinema many big stars and professional ways of working.

h: Khyber Darra: stories of ordinary people, big questions
dek: On Jankipul, Deepak Girkar reads Pankaj Subeer's short story collection 'Khyber Darra' (Khyber Pass), which won the Kalinga Literary Festival's Book of the Year award this year.
body: Indore-based critic Deepak Girkar has written on Jankipul about Pankaj Subeer's short story collection 'Khyber Darra' (Khyber Pass). Published by Rajpal & Sons, the 176-page book was chosen Book of the Year by the Kalinga Literary Festival in 2026. According to the critic, these stories rise from the life of the common man and, while staying in the present, often collide with the past through memory.

The title story has neighbourhoods divided by religion, where communal violence spreads fast and politicians and goons profit from hatred. In the middle of this, a disabled father and his daughter slowly change a hate-filled man through their compassion. Girkar sees its essence in humanity and the possibility of change.

He finds 'Hare Teen Ki Chhat' (The Green Tin Roof) the most memorable: Arjun, the watchman's son at a rest house in Pachmarhi, and Meera, an officer's daughter, who returns forty years later to find that Arjun has named his restaurant after her. 'Veerbahutiyan Chali Gayin' (The Red Velvet Mites Are Gone) carries, along with innocent love, grief at the loss of forests and folk beliefs.

Several stories are about bodies on the margins. In 'Deh Dhare Ka Dand' (The Punishment of Having a Body), two boys suffer harassment without understanding homosexuality; 'Nirling' (Without Gender) is about the pain of third gender people. The collector in 'Kabir Maya Papani' (Kabir: Maya the Sinner) weeps more over missing his commission from the liquor shop auction than over his mother's death. In 'Ijazat@Ghodadongri' (Permission@Ghodadongri), Dhara leaves her Brahmin husband for an Adivasi (indigenous) man and does not apologise.

The review is almost entirely praise, pauses little on weaknesses of craft, and says at the start that there are nine stories but later mentions eleven. Still, this map of the stories shows what questions Subeer is grappling with.
nazar: Look at this collection's range: a riot, corrupt bureaucracy, gay teenagers, the third gender, a woman who sees an Adivasi area as the centre of the country. Hindi fiction becomes a record of its time only when it goes into these dark corners of small towns. What jars is that our reviewing is still stuck between praise and summary, with little courage for criticism.
sawal: Will Hindi reviewing ever move beyond praise?
ref: Pankaj Subeer
Hindi fiction writer and editor from Sehore (Madhya Pradesh). 'Khyber Darra' is his short story collection, which won the Kalinga Literary Festival's Book of the Year award in 2026.
Ghodadongri
An Adivasi-majority town and railway station in Betul district of Madhya Pradesh. The story's heroine calls it, rather than Nagpur, the country's true geographical centre.

h: Have the gods cursed me? Fifteen women's voices from Prakrit
dek: On Sadaneera, Kumar Mangalam has translated fifteen short Prakrit poems into Hindi, in which desire, separation and the body speak without any hesitation.
body: Sadaneera, a magazine of world poetry, has published Hindi translations of fifteen poems from Prakrit. The translator, Kumar Mangalam, is a poet and translator of the new generation. There is no introduction on the page; the poems are placed directly before the reader. Some carry the names of women poets, such as Vikatanitamba, Vijja, Jaghanachapala and Shilabhattarika, while the rest are listed under the names of different satsais (collections of seven hundred verses).

The speaker in most of these poems is a woman, and she does not hide her desire. The first poem has a mango tree outside the door whose fragrance stirs such an ache in the body that she asks whether the gods have cursed her. Another poem has a rainy night, the city's lanes washed clean, the husband away in a far land, and the woman happy with this freedom.

The poem listed under Shilabhattarika's name has spring returning after years, scattered jasmine and kadamba branches swaying in the wind, and the memory of a first meeting in a sugarcane field on the bank of the Narmada. Elsewhere there is waiting on a forest path covered with autumn leaves, and words left unsaid as a lamp goes out.

Some poems take on society directly. In one, a woman says people will talk, let them talk, and calls her lover close even during her period. In one, there is a question about saffron threads stuck to a chest, and both burst out laughing. In the last poem, after the lover leaves in the morning, there is emptiness everywhere, from the temple to the lane.
These lines come from a tradition fifteen hundred to two thousand years old, but their language feels of today. The translation is short and clear, and that is its strength.
nazar: We often assume that speaking openly of a woman's desire is a gift of modernity. These Prakrit women poets break that illusion. In an age when talking about the body and menstruation is still made a matter of shame, these old voices seem even bolder. The only regret is that a short introduction on sources and context with the translation would have shown the reader the way.
sawal: Was our tradition more open, or is our memory short?
ref: Prakrit
A group of ancient Indian people's languages that ran parallel to Sanskrit. Poems of love and household life, like the Satavahana king Hala's 'Gaha Sattasai', were composed in it.
Satsai
A collection of seven hundred verses. Beginning with the Prakrit 'Gaha Sattasai', this tradition reached Hindi in the Bihari Satsai.
